skills.when_to_use: Use when the question demands precise cross-video correspondence, discrimination, or selection among videos/options, recognizable from the question text and video list alone: questions that reference labeled object IDs across synchronized camera views and ask where one object is when an event involving another occurs, or ask for a labeled object's trajectory, position, or visibility; questions that name a time interval or timestamp in one video and ask for the functionally equivalent step or interval in another, or otherwise require a time-interval answer about a specific visible action; questions asking which of several videos, segments, or options exhibits a stated property, state, error, or ending condition; or questions asking which action is performed incorrectly a stated number of times across videos of the same activity. Do not use for open narrative inference questions (e.g., predicting a middle segment from a beginning and an ending) where summarizing each video separately suffices.
skills.strategy: Apply this procedure in order; it overrides the default single-pass workflow. Stage 1, neutral first acquisition: for each referenced video, issue one per-video instruction asking for a timestamped, purely descriptive account of the relevant objects, actions, or scenes — every occurrence with its visible start and end seconds and visible attributes — and a complete timeline of all occurrences of the target action across the whole video, not just the first instance found. Do not embed the answer options, a yes/no verdict request, or an expected conclusion in the first pass: verdict-seeking instructions bias the analyst toward confirming or denying the premise instead of reporting what is visible. For synchronized multi-view questions with visually labeled object IDs, state in each instruction that a referenced ID is shown with a colored box only during that object's first visible second, and ask the agent to report any colored box near the start of the video, the object inside it, and that object's appearance, position and motion thereafter; brief label windows are easily missed, so ask explicitly. For a referenced event at a stated time, request that interval plus several seconds of surrounding context. For a property-selection question (which video shows or ends with X), ask each video for a raw description of the relevant moments and decide the property yourself from those raw details, never from the analyst's own verdict. Stage 2, consistency gate before answering: compare all accumulated reports against each other and against the required output format. Raise a flag when: (a) two reports about the same object or moment directly conflict; (b) a single-video report says a question-referenced labeled object is not visible or unidentifiable — the question presupposes the label exists, so treat this as a probable perception miss, not confirmed absence; (c) a report is degenerate relative to the required answer, such as a single point timestamp where an interval with distinct start and end is required, or an event or anchor located at exactly 0.0 seconds or at a selected clip's start boundary, which often reflects the clip edge rather than the true event; (d) a report's raw visual description contradicts its own interpretive conclusion; (e) a candidate interval or event time came from a joint watch whose total selected duration was long relative to the detail sought, so sampling was too sparse to localize it reliably; (f) an observation states a relation or position that matches none of the answer options. Stage 3, targeted re-acquisition when flagged: do not answer from flagged evidence and do not guess from assumptions about how such question sets are constructed. For a label miss or identity conflict across synchronized views, run one joint watch of the relevant videos using short clips around each view's opening seconds (where the colored boxes appear) and around any claimed moment, keeping the total selected duration small so sampling stays dense; ask the visual model to report the colored boxes, the labeled objects' appearance, and the raw spatial layout at the question's target moment, without stating which option is correct. Never answer a 'not visible', 'stays in place', or similar default option on the basis of failed acquisition alone; such an option is supported only by a dense re-watch that positively establishes the object's absence or stillness after its label window has been densely checked. When an observation matches no option, do not convert the mismatch into an answer by elimination (for example, inferring 'not visible' because an observed direction is unlisted); re-watch densely around the claimed moment and the label window, and map the raw layout to an option only if the re-watch still supports it. For any time-interval answer, before submitting it run one dense confirmation watch on a tight window covering the candidate interval plus a few seconds before and after, asking for the action's full visible start and end seconds, how long it visibly continues, and whether the same action occurs at any other time; adjust or reject the candidate accordingly. For an anchor claimed at 0.0 seconds or a clip boundary, densely re-watch the first several seconds and any later candidate moments before accepting it. Stage 4, final answer from raw description: answer only from the described visual content, not from an analyst's or visual model's verdict phrase, not from elimination reasoning over the option list, and not from plausibility priors about intended answers. If the question presupposes exactly one correct option but all raw descriptions still fail to support any option, choose the option whose support rests on the strongest described visual details, re-read the raw descriptions for a detail that resolves the choice, and record the residual uncertainty in the answer's reason. Never substitute a discussion of missing evidence for the requested answer representation.
